look_here_first: RICE CUTGRASS: on wet stream edges inspect a source-verified airy loose panicle of narrow rice-grain spikelets plus rough grass blades. Use a lens, NEVER run bare fingertips along edges: backward-pointing sharp tiny LEAF-MARGIN teeth need their own 10–20× measured macro. Actual newly sourced photos show a HAIRY CULM NODE (not ligule), ROUGH SHEATH, REAL BLADE–SHEATH LIGULE, full inflorescence and a true opened one-flowered SPIKELET with lemma and palea. For white cutgrass L. virginica check the lowest branch junction (L. oryzoides frequently ≥2 branches) and mature ~4–6.5-mm spikelets rather than relying on wetland habitat. Austrian external photos are not independent Hays vouchers.

best_field_traits: Long rhizomatous wetland perennial with spreading, often decumbent, rooted stems.
Rough leaf sheaths; blades often ~5–15 mm wide with BACKWARD-POINTING microscopic teeth along both edges.
Open terminal/axillary panicles often have 2 or more branches at the lowest nodes (important contrast with Leersia virginica).
Narrow 4–6.5 mm flattened one-flowered spikelets, glumes absent or inconspicuous.
Rhizomes often long, with scales not closely overlapping.
crew_field_check: Handle rough edges carefully with lens/forceps; don't deliberately drag fingers along the blade.
Check exact same plant for 2+ basal panicle branches and 4–6.5 mm narrow mature spikelet.
Separate 1-flowered Leersia with obscure glumes from similar wetland grasses and related cutgrasses.
Don't claim species by habitat alone; capture collar and rhizome only if visible.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: WHOLE: same rooted stand in shallow water/creek margin; multiple branches attached to base, habitat in frame.
LEAF MARGIN: strong 10× macro with 1 mm reference showing tiny DOWNWARD/RETRORSE sharp hairs or teeth; avoid running bare fingers along the edge.
TRUE LIGULE: junction of blade and sheath, roughly 0.5–1.5 mm short membranous edge with scale.
SHEATH / NODE: rough sheath surface and any small bands of hairs at attached stem nodes.
PANICLE: clearly show 2 or more branches from the LOWEST main flowering-head node, if present; contrast with white cutgrass single branch.
SPIKELET: 4–6.5 mm narrow compressed unit against millimeter scale, both faces and glume-free base/attachment shown.
RHIZOME: exposed long creeping underground stem with spaced non-overlapping scales, only where collecting is allowed; restore exposed soil.
OPTIONAL: reduced upper sheath-enclosed axillary flowerhead (cleistogamous panicle), if found on same plant.
second_pass_field_teaching_20261022: 1. Identify a wet-bank plant stand and an intact flowing/branching inflorescence; treat habitat as context, not proof of species.
2. Follow the main PANICLE RACHIS from uppermost leaf to its LOWEST first branching nodes. Count 2+ genuinely attached primary branches, not crossing free-floating stems.
3. Examine the stem NODE: a separate fuzzy HAIR RING encircles the joint. The sl21 photo is a proper documented hairy node.

4. Inspect the ROUGH SHEATH in sl22; it is NOT a photo of the blade margin. To prove retrorse blade-edge sawteeth, collect a safe specimen sample with forceps and photograph it at 10–20× with 1mm scale. Do not stroke it on skin.
5. At the leaf blade/sheath junction photograph the short pale TRUE MEMBRANOUS LIGULE from face and side. The sl23 photo is authentic but not calibration proof of 0.5–1 mm length.
6. Look at the one-flowered elliptical, flattened spikelets, generally 4.2–6.5 mm (check a true 1-mm ruler). Contrast small L. virginica, typically 2.2–4 mm and often one low panicle branch.

7. Use sl30 actual photo labeling for the LEMMA and PALEA, the enclosing one-floret structures. L. oryzoides spikelets lack the conspicuous ordinary basal GLUMES; do not put arrow labels for absent structures.

8. Look at the separate sl31 intentionally OPENED spikelet. Crew teach-back: point to one node, sheath, ligule, low panicle branching, spikelet, Lem/Pal; if teeth or measurements remain hidden, label provisional.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Rice cutgrass L. oryzoides: notably retrorse-prickly/rough leaves and sheaths; mature spreading panicle usually 2+ branches at lowermost nodes (verify their COMMON point on rachis); oblong flat 1-flowered spikelets usually 4.2–6.5 × 1.3–1.7 mm and short membranous ligule 0.5–1 mm. White cutgrass L. virginica: usually smoother or less harshly rough sheaths, often a single panicle branch at a lowermost node, smaller spikelets ~2.2–4 mm that generally overlap little along the branchlets (in contrast to the more overlapping spikelets of L. oryzoides); count mature branching and measure spikelets rather than rely on roughness. L. lenticularis has wider, almost disk- or lens-shaped spikelets, not narrow 'rice grains'. Zizaniopsis and Zizania have different flowering structure; Texas wild-rice is a protected aquatic plant and must not be handled or uprooted for comparisons. Paspalum spikelets are generally arranged differently; inspect the actual glumes/lemmas, not just habitat.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Usually more delicate with smoother or only moderately rough leaf sheaths. Flowering head generally has ONE branch at a low node rather than two or more; small spikelets (~2.4–4 mm) usually barely overlapping on the branchlets; short closely overlapping rhizome scales. Mature paired-branch and spikelet counts are more reliable than wet habitat alone.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Whole panicle lower branching node and single spikelet with mm reference; correct source-labelled specimen.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Spikelets are broad and round or lens-shaped rather than elongate narrow 'rice grains'; may be nearly circular and often look like little disks. Large leaf blades may be similarly rough, so seek mature spikelet dimensions and outline.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Spikelets from face and edge, with mm ruler and attached pedicel.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Much taller robust marsh grass with broad blades and a large branching panicle whose reproductive spikelets are organized differently; compare whole plant scale and flowering structures, not sharp leaf edges alone.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Whole stand and size comparison plus panicle close-up.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Aquatic perennial from flowing river channels with dramatically different pollen- and seed-bearing branches. Do not mistake any narrow water-edge grass leaf for this endangered localized aquatic grass. Species diagnosis and stewardship need the actual inflorescence and habitat context.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Legal non-disturbing habitat and clear flowering anatomy; never uproot protected wild-rice.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Many one-sided racemes bear two-flowered spikelets and a membranous ligule. Leersia typically has very rough leaf surfaces/margins, more flexible open panicle branches, and flattened one-flowered spikelets with no evident glumes.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Matched leaf-edge and flowering branch + single spikelet macro.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: LOOK AT THE EDGES OF THE LEAVES (CAREFULLY): rice cutgrass has extremely ROUGH, backward-pointing sharp microscopic teeth on blade margins and often sheaths. In wetland stands it makes open branching panicles of small flattened grain-like one-flowered spikelets (often ~4–6 mm), with very short membranous true ligule. For L. oryzoides versus white cutgrass, compare the LOWEST panicle node (often 2 or more branches) and measured mature spikelets; do not identify by roughness alone.
photo_targets: WHOLE: same rooted stand in shallow water/creek margin; multiple branches attached to base, habitat in frame.
LEAF MARGIN: strong 10× macro with 1 mm reference showing tiny DOWNWARD/RETRORSE sharp hairs or teeth; avoid running bare fingers along the edge.
TRUE LIGULE: junction of blade and sheath, roughly 0.5–1.5 mm short membranous edge with scale.
SHEATH / NODE: rough sheath surface and any small bands of hairs at attached stem nodes.
PANICLE: clearly show 2 or more branches from the LOWEST main flowering-head node, if present; contrast with white cutgrass single branch.
SPIKELET: 4–6.5 mm narrow compressed unit against millimeter scale, both faces and glume-free base/attachment shown.
RHIZOME: exposed long creeping underground stem with spaced non-overlapping scales, only where collecting is allowed; restore exposed soil.
OPTIONAL: reduced upper sheath-enclosed axillary flowerhead (cleistogamous panicle), if found on same plant.

eight_step_crew_sequence: 1. Identify a wet-bank plant stand and an intact flowing/branching inflorescence; treat habitat as context, not proof of species.
2. Follow the main PANICLE RACHIS from uppermost leaf to its LOWEST first branching nodes. Count 2+ genuinely attached primary branches, not crossing free-floating stems.
3. Examine the stem NODE: a separate fuzzy HAIR RING encircles the joint. The sl21 photo is a proper documented hairy node.

4. Inspect the ROUGH SHEATH in sl22; it is NOT a photo of the blade margin. To prove retrorse blade-edge sawteeth, collect a safe specimen sample with forceps and photograph it at 10–20× with 1mm scale. Do not stroke it on skin.
5. At the leaf blade/sheath junction photograph the short pale TRUE MEMBRANOUS LIGULE from face and side. The sl23 photo is authentic but not calibration proof of 0.5–1 mm length.
6. Look at the one-flowered elliptical, flattened spikelets, generally 4.2–6.5 mm (check a true 1-mm ruler). Contrast small L. virginica, typically 2.2–4 mm and often one low panicle branch.

7. Use sl30 actual photo labeling for the LEMMA and PALEA, the enclosing one-floret structures. L. oryzoides spikelets lack the conspicuous ordinary basal GLUMES; do not put arrow labels for absent structures.

8. Look at the separate sl31 intentionally OPENED spikelet. Crew teach-back: point to one node, sheath, ligule, low panicle branching, spikelet, Lem/Pal; if teeth or measurements remain hidden, label provisional.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Rice cutgrass — 5-photo crew check (do not use your bare fingers on the serrated edge)
steps: Photograph a Hays-area wet-site culm from rooted base to its attached flowering panicle. The full gallery already contains a genuine separately excavated rice-cutgrass root crown and rhizomes, but it is not a connected Hays specimen.

Check the LEAF EDGE using macro and backlight: tiny retrorse (backward-pointing) spinules along the edge and rough sheath, with a 1-mm scale. This is the hallmark missing photo; never feel across the blade with bare skin.

Photograph the LOWEST panicle branching node with the central axis and ALL departing primary branches in focus. Rice cutgrass typically has 2 or more at this node; gallery panel 2 now points to the lowest visible branching ZONE, but does not resolve the actual 2+ same-node branch count.

Put a mature spikelet under 10–20× alongside a millimeter rule: narrow flattened one-flowered unit typically ~4.2–6.5 mm; inspect its awnless profile and reduced/absent true glumes, not individual structures guessed from a hand-scale photo.

Open a FRESH blade–sheath junction for the 0.5–1 mm membranous ligule. Compare source-identified white cutgrass's often single lower branch and smaller spikelets, and disk-like catchfly cutgrass. Photograph without damaging protected wetland grasses.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Leaf-edge retrorse prickles + mature open panicle + typically 2+ branches at basal PANICLE nodes + narrow measured 4.2–6.5 mm spikelets strongly support L. oryzoides; no single one proves the species.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: The archived IRIIS root/rhizome photograph is real and useful, but is not a Hays-area root-to-flowering-head voucher. The USGS blade-edge photo shows edge context, not independently direction-proven 10–20× teeth. Photo 2's broad leaves may belong to neighboring grass stems. No existing photograph proves 2+ branches co-originating at the lowest panicle node, the actual glumeless insertion, or an individually measured ligule. Preserve Joey's source-specific rights hold and avoid touching sharp leaf edges with bare hands.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · SHARP LEAF EDGE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Look for backward-pointing microscopic blade-margin teeth — never feel with bare fingers
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panel 12 (Larry Allain, USGS public domain) shows the actual leaf-blade edge at ordinary photo scale; panel 4 shows microscopic backward-curved prickles on the SHEATH, not the blade. Neither establishes the direction or size of individual BLADE-margin teeth. A taxon-confirmed 10–20× blade-edge macro with a 1-mm reference remains required; never feel the sharp edge with bare fingers.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · LOWEST PANICLE NODE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Count branches sharing the lowest flowering-head node
field_id_short_tiles.details: Rice cutgrass often has two or more primary branches at the lowest panicle node; white cutgrass often has one. Panel 1 now has a verified arrow to the LOWEST VISIBLE BRANCHING ZONE, but the source photograph does NOT resolve whether two branches actually originate from one node. Photograph the common attachment in front and side views; crossing branches are not a count.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: A real membranous ligule is photographed with a 5-mm scale; its free apex still needs measurement
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panel 5 (Stefan.lefnaer sl23, CC BY-SA 4.0) actually shows the pale membranous ligule and an original printed 5-mm reference bar; the existing arrow identifies the visible flap. Published ligule length is roughly 0.5–1.5 mm (some treatments 0.5–1 mm), but the free apex and exact individual length are NOT independently measurable from this view. Obtain a perpendicular opened collar macro with 1-mm divisions; panel 3 is a hairy STEM NODE, not a ligule.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TRUE LIGULE AND 5-MM BAR PHOTOGRAPHED — FREE APEX / 1-MM MEASUREMENT HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · ONE-FLOWERED RICE SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: Scaled flattened spikelet photos exist; verify actual glumeless insertion and lemma/palea
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 8 and 11 show actual detached source-identified spikelets with original 3-mm and 5-mm bars; panel 10 shows spikelet edges with a 10-mm bar, and panel 7 carries the photographer's Lem/Pal labels. Panel 15 is a single isolated flattened spikelet without a ruler. These photographs support anatomy and relative scale, NOT a measured 4.2–6.5 mm individual, independently confirmed absent/reduced basal glumes, or the same-specimen lemma/palea boundary. Do not invent glume arrows or a species measurement from a printed bar alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-LABELED SCALED SPIKELET VIEWS — GLUMELESS BASE / INDIVIDUAL MEASUREMENT HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT WHITE CUTGRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Combine lowest-branch count, spikelet size and leaf-edge anatomy
field_id_short_tiles.details: Leersia virginica often has one lowest primary panicle branch and smaller approximately 2.2–4 mm spikelets; overlap and obscured attachments mean no single clue confirms either species. L. lenticularis has broader lentil-like spikelets. Keep protected Texas wild-rice and other wetland grasses undisturbed.
